opus-5.5.text:
When I started my PhD, I honestly felt a bit like an outsider. The traditional robotics community at that time was built on a very strong foundation of modeling, control theory, planning, and state estimation. People cared deeply about guarantees: you write down the dynamics, you analyze stability, you prove that your controller converges. That culture is really rigorous, and I have a lot of respect for it.

My interests were coming more from the learning side. I was excited by what was happening in deep learning and in vision, and I kept asking whether robots could acquire skills from data instead of from carefully hand-engineered models. At that point, that wasn't fully mainstream in robotics. Some people saw learning as a black box: it works in simulation, maybe, or in a narrow demo, but you can't trust it on real hardware, and you can't explain why it fails.

So in the beginning I saw my work as sitting at the boundary. I wasn't trying to replace the classical approaches. I was trying to find the places where they struggled, like contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, or messy unstructured environments where writing an accurate model is almost impossible, and to ask whether data could fill that gap.

That boundary position was uncomfortable at first. When you submit papers, reviewers from the classical side ask, "Where's the analysis? Where's the guarantee?" Reviewers from the ML side ask, "Why is your benchmark so small? Why only one robot?" You get criticized from both directions. Over time, though, I came to see it as an advantage. Classical robotics taught me to respect the physical system: hardware is unforgiving, and evaluation on real robots matters. The learning community taught me to think about scale and generalization.

Looking back, the field moved a lot during those years. What felt like a fringe direction gradually became one of the central conversations in robotics. But I still think the most interesting work happens when you take both traditions seriously instead of treating it as a fight between them.

r001.rationale: Kay Ke describes feeling like an outsider and says learning-based robotics was not fully mainstream, placing their work at the boundary of the traditional robotics community.

fable-5.1.text:
When I started my PhD, honestly, I felt like I was sitting at the edge of the room. The traditional robotics community at that time was very much about control, planning, state estimation, kinematics. Very rigorous, very model-based. You write down the dynamics, you prove stability, you design a controller. That was the culture, and I respected it a lot.

My interests were drifting toward learning. I wanted robots to pick things up from data, from interaction, rather than from a hand-written model. And in those early years that was treated a bit like a side hobby. People would say, okay, learning is interesting, but will it ever work on a real arm? Can you give me a guarantee? And I didn't have good answers.

So I did something a little schizophrenic. On paper I tried to speak the language of the community. I would frame the problem in terms of manipulation, in terms of grasping, in terms of an actual physical task that a roboticist would recognize. But underneath, the method was learned. I tried to sneak learning in through the back door, basically.

In hindsight that tension was actually healthy. The traditional community forced me to care about the physical world, about contact, about real hardware failing in ugly ways. The learning side gave me tools to handle the messiness that models can't capture. I think a lot of people from my generation lived in that gap, and the gap is where the interesting work happened.

r001.rationale: Kay says they felt “at the edge of the room” and that learning was treated as a “side hobby,” conveying that their research occupied a niche position in traditional robotics.

astra-6.text: When I entered school, I wasn’t quite sure where my research would fit within traditional robotics. I saw a community with a lot of established ways of framing problems, and I was still figuring out which questions I wanted to ask. So initially, it was less about finding a particular category for my work and more about understanding the field—what people cared about, what assumptions they made, and where I might be able to contribute.
